subject: knight
pitch: A fantasy knight in battle-worn plate armour. A great helm with a narrow eye slit and a tall crimson plume, layered shoulder plates etched with gold filigree, a deep-blue surcoat with a silver griffin emblem, a tall kite shield bearing the same griffin, and a broadsword. Dents and scratches tell of many battles, and a torn crimson cape hangs from the shoulders.
reasoning:
I'm planning a stylized low-poly knight model using the 3js builder SDK, picturing a great helm with a tall crimson plume, layered shoulder plates with gold filigree, and a deep-blue surcoat bearing a silver griffin emblem.

Within the constraints (1000 parts, 60k triangles, 160 joints, 64 flat colours, ~1.9m tall facing +Z), I'm sketching a rigged skeleton with hips as root, spine, neck, head, and limb joints like shoulderL/elbowL/wristL and hipL/kneeL/ankleL, setting the rest pose with arms slightly extended, sword in the right hand, and the griffin shield on the left arm. I'm also noting details like dents, scratches, and a torn crimson cape, and need to double-check the SDK's coordinate conventions before building further.

Importing the SDK functions...

I'm sketching out the vertical proportions of the knight figure, planning rough y-coordinates for feet, knees, hips, chest, shoulders, neck, and helm so the whole model reads as a coherent standing figure around two meters tall.

Now I'm designing the great helm as a flat-topped cylinder with a crimson plume on top, and starting to lay out the skeleton — a root hips joint with a spine chain curving up through waist and chest using a catmull path, thinking through how to name each chain segment so parenting stays clean.

For the neck and head, I'm deciding simple joints are safer than a chain since the armor hides the neck anyway — a neck joint rising from the chest, then a head joint centered inside the helm, each tagged with the appropriate role.

For orientation, joints without their own aim or direction simply inherit the parent's orientation, which simplifies things since I'll always pass parent explicitly.

Now for the shoulders and arms, I'm planning to build each arm as a chain from shoulder through elbow to wrist to a hand-tip joint, using a four-point path to get three spans with matching names for each segment.

For legs, I'm figuring out the naming convention: a path of hip-knee-ankle with two names produces two span joints plus an added tip joint for the foot, so I need to make sure the number of names aligns correctly with spans plus the extra tip joint.

For the limbs themselves, I'm considering using IK-based limb helpers that compute intermediate joints (like knees) from root, target, and segment lengths, with bend direction controlling which way the knee or elbow points, and planning to use a straight-down target with forward bend for standing legs.

I'll just use explicit hip, knee, ankle, and toe points chained into joints for each leg, skipping IK entirely since the limb geometry handles the visual bend. For the armor, I'm thinking cuisses and greaves as boxy loft/sweep sections with sabatons for feet, plus pauldrons, vambraces, and gauntlets on the arms. For the rest pose, I'll give the knight a slight A-pose: left arm raised forward holding the kite shield out in front, while the right sword arm extends down and outward.

For the sword, a classic planted pose reads well -- blade angled down with the tip grazing or just touching the floor beside the right foot, keeping within the floor-contact tolerance while staying visually dynamic yet still neutral enough for a rest pose.

Now I'm working out the shield: a kite shape mounted on the left forearm, sized proportionally with a pointed bottom, built as an extruded part facing forward and slightly outward. Since extrusion only supports flat colors, I'm planning to add the griffin emblem as a decal applied directly onto the shield's flat surface, positioning and sizing it to fit within the kite outline.

I need to design the griffin as an SVG with a transparent background so the shield's painted base color shows through around the silhouette, giving a classic heraldic look of a silver griffin on a colored field. The SVG itself requires careful path work to render a recognizable griffin -- head with beak and ear, wings, body, tail, and claws -- within a compact 100x100 viewBox.

For the surcoat, I'm placing a second griffin decal on the chest, using the surcoat's sweep geometry as the decal target and positioning the projection point and direction so the grid wraps correctly onto the torso's front surface.

Since the ray only considers meshes in the target list, passing surcoat alone ensures it hits that outer layer first, which makes sense since the surcoat drapes over the breastplate and only the arm, neck, and leg plates stay visible.

Now I'm settling on the palette: steel grays, a deep blue for the surcoat, gold accents, crimson for the plume, dark leather and near-black for straps and eye slits, plus a shadow tone. I'm also considering texture paint functions like mottle, scales, and grain to add surface detail.

For battle wear I'm mixing steel with darker patches to suggest scratches and dents, possibly using grain streaks for scratch texture and thinking through whether dents need actual geometry displacement or just decals. For the gold filigree on the pauldrons, I'm leaning toward an SVG decal applied over the curved plate surface rather than trying to procedurally generate the pattern with noise-based paint. For the great helm's eye slit, I'm picturing a narrow dark box set into a cylindrical helm shape, possibly built as a frustum or lofted sweep.

I should also add a T-visor look, with a horizontal slit and vertical rib for reinforcement, kept stylized. For the helm shape itself, I'm considering a lathe profile with 8 segments to get a faceted octagonal dome—sharp corners will crease naturally since they exceed the smoothing threshold, giving a flat-top great helm effect. I'll center the lathe profile around the head joint, positioning it so the outline's height spans correctly along the axis.

For the plume on top, I'm thinking of a flowing crimson crest—either layered feather-like cards along an arc, or a single extruded flame/feather shape with bevel that arches back over the helm.

Designing plume spine curve...

That messy outline risks self-intersection, so instead I'm reconsidering using cards along a backward-sweeping arc for the plume -- placing frames via `b.along()` with a path and count, then feeding those frames into `b.cards()` with the crimson plume texture.

Let me simplify this: instead of cards, I'll build the plume as a horsehair crest made of a dozen or so thin tapered curved tubes arranged in a fan across the helm's width, arcing upward and back, radii tapering from thick to thin for a stylized crimson hair effect, maybe combined with a few flat extruded fins for added volume.
